near_miss.lead: Weaving a plot / being entangled in wrongdoing
near_miss.why_not: Context and corpus searches distinguish Icelandic reflexive vafist 'become involved' from Homeric transitive weaving of counsel. Homeric parallels Il. 7.324 and Od. 13.386 reinforce the latter formula, but no cognate counsel object or matching construction occurs in the Icelandic anchor. Shared textile imagery alone is insufficient.

The slab partners concern infantry, measurements of rope, and footprints, not trampling or domination. Searches found literal calcato pedibus in Cato Agr. 28.2 and a figurative outside-slab Lucretius parallel (recorded separately); no anchored claim is available.
In Icelandic konur is the subject of mjólka; in Irish blicht belongs with bó and ben is a separate coordinated demand. Cognate woman and milk words do not form the same syntactic collocation.

near_miss.lead: Father and mother / knowing one's parents
near_miss.why_not: Paired kin terms are ordinary genealogy. The Icelandic foster-parent discussion, visiting parents, and two generations of kin differ from Vedic serpent ancestry, healing, earth/sky parentage, and Greek full siblinghood. Even the know-plus-parents match in BS-51117 lacks distinctive inherited phrasing.

near_miss.lead: Two hundreds and adjacent ordinal numerals
near_miss.why_not: The deathbed disclosure of hidden wealth and Vedic enumeration of cattle gifts share productive numeral grammar, not a distinctive phrase. The other bundle enumerates sons versus years, days, walls and tolls. Numerical agreement alone does not establish poetic inheritance.

Both nouns occur in a weather list, but Icelandic negative coordination differs from Lucretius' longer meteorological catalogue. Searches recover the same Latin line and another Icelandic storm list in Viglundur s546. Nothing distinguishes inherited wording from ordinary descriptions of cold weather.

near_miss.lead: Dark night with cognate darkness vocabulary
near_miss.why_not: Germanic myrkt af nótt is an impersonal predication with causal af, recurrent also in Grettir s800 and Jomsvikingar s1304. Serbian gives vocative night full of darkness and an epithet/genitive construction. Despite cognate mergʷ and nókʷts, darkness of night is predictable, and the late Serbian lyric contexts do not secure a common formula.

near_miss.lead: Recognizing the wolf by its ears
near_miss.why_not: The Greek anchor has the personal name Lycus and a verb of hearing, not a wolf's ears. Searches for lupus plus auris found no match; the indexed Latin wolf examples do not reproduce the proverb. A recalled Latin wolf-by-the-ears saying is not used as an unattested support witness.

near_miss.lead: Slaying cattle as a hostile act
near_miss.why_not: Vedic gām haṃsi and Icelandic kýr til bana concern cattle killed or threatened, but the Icelandic death noun occurs in a result phrase with wounded cattle, not as the cognate killing verb. Livestock destruction is too generic; the contexts and constructions do not justify an inherited phrase.

search_lead.cognate: Icelandic fótum and Latin pedibus continue pṓds (oblique ped-), both plural in the underfoot image.
search_lead.argument: The Icelandic church's freedom is figuratively trampled under feet; Lucretius presents religio as put beneath feet and crushed. This is a closer outside-slab figure than any assigned partner. It is a review lead only: the trampling verb is renewed/noncognate here, the religious evaluations differ, and medieval Christian/Latin transmission or independent metaphor could explain the resemblance. No claim of secure PIE inheritance.
